claim: Encoding precision in visual working memory decreases with the number of encoded items.
source: Encoding precision in visual working memory decreases with the number of encoded items.
evidence: This is a well-established empirical finding cited in the introduction with references to Ma et al., 2014 and Luck and Vogel, 2013.

claim: The brain minimizes a weighted sum of an error-based behavioral cost and a neural encoding cost.
source: Here, we propose a normative theory for such set size effects: the brain minimizes a weighted sum of an error-based behavioral cost and a neural encoding cost.
evidence: This is the central theoretical proposal of the paper, presented as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Set size effects are mediated by probing probability.
source: Notably, these effects are mediated by probing probability, which aligns with previous empirical findings.
evidence: The paper cites previous empirical findings and presents model predictions that align with this claim.

claim: The model accounts well for effects of both set size and probing probability on encoding precision in nine delayed-estimation experiments.
source: The model accounts well for effects of both set size and probing probability on encoding precision in nine delayed-estimation experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting results presented in the Results section.

claim: The total amount of invested resource can vary non-monotonically with set size.
source: Moreover, we find support for the prediction that the total amount of invested resource can vary non-monotonically with set size.
evidence: This is supported by empirical analysis of data from experiments E2 and E4-E6.

claim: It is sometimes optimal to encode only a subset or even none of the relevant items in a task.
source: Finally, we show that it is sometimes optimal to encode only a subset or even none of the relevant items in a task.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical analysis and supported by model predictions.

claim: Cognitive limitations arise from rational cost minimization rather than from constraints.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that cognitive "limitations" arise from rational cost minimization rather than from constraints.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Models with a fixed amount of resource generally predict that the encoding precision per item is inversely proportional to set size.
source: Models with a fixed amount of resource generally predict that the encoding precision per item (defined as inverse variance of the encoding error) is inversely proportional to set size.
evidence: This is a statement about the predictions of existing models in the literature.

claim: The prediction of inverse proportionality between encoding precision and set size is often inconsistent with empirical data.
source: This prediction is often inconsistent with empirical data, which is the reason that more recent studies instead use a power law to describe set size effects (Bays et al., 2009; Bays and Husain, 2008; van den Berg et al., 2012; van den Berg et al., 2014; Devkar et al., 2015; Elmore et al., 2011; Mazyar et al., 2012; Wilken and Ma, 2004; Donkin et al., 2016; Keshvari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Power-law models provide excellent fits to experimental data but lack a principled motivation.
source: These models tend to provide excellent fits to experimental data, but they have been criticized for lacking a principled motivation (Oberauer et al., 2016; Oberauer and Lin, 2017): they accurately describe how memory precision depends on set size, but not why these effects are best described by a power law – or why they exist at all.
evidence: This is supported by citations to critical papers and is a motivation for the current work.

claim: Neural coding is costly.
source: The starting point of our theory is the principle that neural coding is costly (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Lennie, 2003; Sterling and Laughlin, 2015), which may have pressured the brain to trade off the behavioral benefits of high precision against the cost of the resource invested in stimulus encoding (Pestilli and Carrasco, 2005; Lennie, 2003; Ma and Huang, 2009; Christie and Schrater, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: Increasing the amount of resource spent on encoding will reduce the expected behavioral cost but simultaneously increase the expected neural cost.
source: Generally, increasing the amount of resource spent on encoding will reduce the expected behavioral cost, but simultaneously increase the expected neural cost.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the theoretical framework.

claim: Fisher information provides a lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator.
source: This measure provides a lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator (Cover and Thomas, 2005; Ly et al., 2017) and is a common tool in the study of theoretical limits on stimulus coding and discrimination (Abbott and Dayan, 1999).
evidence: This is a well-established mathematical property supported by citations.

claim: There is item-to-item and trial-to-trial variation in precision.
source: Moreover, we assume that there is item-to-item and trial-to-trial variation in precision (Fougnie et al., 2012; van den Berg et al., 2012; van den Berg et al., 2014; Keshvari et al., 2013; van den Berg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: For many choices of spike variability, including Poisson-like variability, Fisher information J is proportional to the trial-averaged neural spiking rate.
source: For many choices of spike variability, including the common one of Poisson-like variability (Ma et al., 2006), Fisher information J of a stimulus encoded in a neural population is proportional to the trial-averaged neural spiking rate (Paradiso, 1988; Seung and Sompolinsky, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical neuroscience literature.

claim: The resource-rational model provides a principled explanation of set size effects without sacrificing quality of fit compared to one of the best available descriptive models of VWM.
source: Hence, the resource-rational model provides a principled explanation of set size effects without sacrificing quality of fit compared to one of the best available descriptive models of VWM.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results using AIC.

claim: The resource-rational model fits better than a model in which the total amount of resource is fixed and divided equally across items.
source: We find that the resource-rational model also fits better than a model in which the total amount of resource is fixed and divided equally across items (ΔAIC = 13.9 ± 1.4).
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: The estimated resource values in the non-parametric model closely match the optimal values in the rational model.
source: An examination of the fitted parameter values corroborates this finding: the estimated resource values in the non-parametric model closely match the optimal values in the rational model (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison in Figure 3C.

claim: The total amount of resource is higher at set size 3 than at set sizes 1 and 6.
source: These tests reveal strong evidence that the total amount of resource is higher at set size 3 than at set sizes 1 (BF+0=1.05·107) and 6 (BF+0=4.02·102).
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian paired t-tests.

claim: Evidence for a possible non-monotonicity in the relation between set size and total encoding resource has not been reported before.
source: To the best of our knowledge, evidence for a possible non-monotonicity in the relation between set size and total encoding resource has not been reported before.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The amount of resource per item should increase as a function of probing probability.
source: Given that the amount of resource per item in E1-E6 decreases with N, a first prediction is that it should increase as a function of pi in E7-E9.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: The estimated total amount of invested resource should vary non-monotonically with probing probability and peak at a value ppeak that is close to 1/Npeak.
source: A second and particularly interesting prediction is that the estimated total amount of invested resource should vary non-monotonically with pi and peak at a value ppeak that is close to 1/Npeak found in E1-E6 (see previous section).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: The predicted value of ppeak is 0.358 ± 0.026.
source: Based on the values of Npeak in experiments E1-E6, we find a prediction ppeak = 0.358 ± 0.026.
evidence: This is computed from the data in E1-E6.

claim: The higher the probing probability of an item, the more precise the subject responses.
source: The subject data show a clear effect of pi: the higher the probing probability of an item, the more precise the subject responses (Figure 4A, top row, black circles).
evidence: This is an empirical observation from experiment E7.

claim: The resource-rational model accounts well for the effect of probing probability on response precision.
source: We find that the resource-rational model, Equation (11), accounts well for this effect (Figure 4A, top row, curves) and does so by increasing the amount of resource as a function of probing probability pi (Figure 4B, left panel, red curves).
evidence: This is supported by model fits shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A Bayesian independent-samples t-test supports the null hypothesis that there is no difference between the observed and predicted peak probing probability.
source: Indeed, a Bayesian independent-samples t-test supports the null hypothesis that there is no difference (BF01 = 4.27).
evidence: This is supported by a Bayesian t-test.

claim: Effects of probing probability in E7-E9 are well accounted for by the same model used to explain effects of set size in E1-E6.
source: In summary, the results in this section show that effects of probing probability in E7-E9 are well accounted for by the same model as we used to explain effects of set size in E1-E6.
evidence: This is a summary of the model fitting results.

claim: Set size effects are mediated by probing probability or, more generally, by item relevance.
source: Regardless of whether total resource is fixed or optimized, this finding provides further support for the suggestion that set size effects are mediated by probing probability (Emrich et al., 2017) or, more generally, by item relevance (Palmer et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results and citations to previous work.

claim: For a fixed-precision model, it is never optimal to invest no resource (p0 = 0).
source: Considering the expected behavioral cost function of a fixed-precision model (a variable-precision model with τ↓0), we can prove that p0 = 0, that is, it is never optimal to invest no resource (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is proven in Appendix 1.

claim: For the variable-precision model, p0 can be greater than 0.
source: For the expected behavioral cost function of the variable-precision model, however, simulations indicate that p0 can be greater than 0 (we were not able to derive this result analytically).
evidence: This is supported by simulations.

claim: The estimated value of p0 (expressed as a percentage) equals 8.86 ± 0.54%.
source: Using the maximum-likelihood parameters obtained from the data in E7-E9, we estimate that p0 (expressed as a percentage) equals 8.86 ± 0.54%.
evidence: This is computed from the fitted model parameters.

claim: For 8 of the 47 subjects, p0 is larger than the lowest probing probability in the experiment.
source: Moreover, we find that for 8 of the 47 subjects, p0 is larger than the lowest probing probability in the experiment, which suggests that these subjects sometimes entirely ignored one or more of the items.
evidence: This is computed from the fitted model parameters.

claim: For subjects with pi<p0, the error distributions look uniform.
source: For these subjects, the error distributions on items with pi<p0 look uniform (see Figure 4C for an example) and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for uniformity did not reject the null hypothesis in any of these cases (p>0.05 in all tests).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection and statistical tests.

claim: There might be a principled reason why people sometimes leave task-relevant items out of visual working memory in delayed-estimation experiments.
source: These results suggest that there might be a principled reason why people sometimes leave task-relevant items out of visual working memory in delayed-estimation experiments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results.

claim: When probing probabilities are equal for all items, the model makes an 'all or none' prediction: all items are encoded when pi>p0 and none are encoded otherwise.
source: In particular, when probing probabilities are equal for all items, the model makes an "all or none" prediction: all items are encoded when pi>p0 and none are encoded otherwise.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model.

claim: The model cannot explain why subjects in tasks with equal probing probabilities sometimes seem to encode a subset of task-relevant items.
source: Hence, the model cannot explain why subjects in tasks with equal probing probabilities sometimes seem to encode a subset of task-relevant items.
evidence: This is a limitation of the model.

claim: In a whole-report delayed-estimation experiment with six items, subjects encoded about half of the items on each trial.
source: For example, a recent study reported that in a whole-report delayed-estimation experiment (pi = 1 for all items), subjects encoded about half of the six presented items on each trial (Adam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from Adam et al., 2017.

claim: The model predicts that subjects do not invest any resource when the feedback threshold is very small or very large.
source: The model predicts that subjects do not invest any resource when the feedback threshold is very small (extremely difficult tasks) or very large (extremely easy tasks), such that the expected absolute estimation error is π/2 (guessing).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: The experimental manipulations in the studies by Zhang and Luck and Nassar et al. may not have been strong enough to measure an effect of incentive on encoding precision.
source: In particular, the simulation results suggest that the experimental manipulations in the studies by Zhang and Luck and Nassar et al. may not have been strong enough to measure an effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of simulation results in the context of previous studies.

claim: Klyszejko and colleagues found a positive relation between the amount of reward associated with an item and response accuracy.
source: For example, Klyszejko and colleagues performed a local change discrimination experiment in which the monetary reward for a correct response depended on which item was probed (Klyszejko et al., 2014). They found a positive relation between the amount of reward associated with an item and response accuracy, which indicates that subjects spent more resource on encoding items with larger potential reward.
evidence: This is cited from Klyszejko et al., 2014.

claim: Divisive normalization would be a likely candidate mechanism for implementing the optimal allocation policy.
source: Some form of divisive normalization (Bays, 2014; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) would be a likely candidate, which is already a key operation in neural models of attention (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009) and visual working memory (Bays, 2014; Wei et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The neural activity associated with the encoding of an item decreases with set size in the lateral intraparietal cortex and superior colliculus.
source: Consistent with the predictions of this theory, empirical work has found that the neural activity associated with the encoding of an item decreases with set size, as observed in for example the lateral intraparietal cortex (Churchland et al., 2008; Balan et al., 2008) and superior colliculus (Basso and Wurtz, 1998).
evidence: This is cited from empirical neuroscience studies.

claim: A modified version of divisive normalization can account for the near-optimal distribution of resources across items with unequal probing probabilities.
source: Moreover, the work by Bays (2014) has shown that a modified version of divisive normalization can account for the near-optimal distribution of resources across items with unequal probing probabilities.
evidence: This is cited from Bays, 2014.

claim: At the neural level, the non-monotonic relation between total resource and set size translates to a prediction of a non-monotonic relation between population-level spiking activity and set size.
source: At the neural level, this translates to a prediction of a non-monotonic relation between population-level spiking activity and set size.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: The theory might apply beyond working memory tasks to attention tasks.
source: Our theory might apply beyond working memory tasks. In particular, it has been speculated that the selectivity of attention arises from a need to balance performance against the costs associated with spiking (Pestilli and Carrasco, 2005; Lennie, 2003). Our theory provides a normative formalism to test this speculation and may thus explain set size effects in attention tasks (Lindsay et al., 1968; Shaw, 1980; Ma and Huang, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the theory.

claim: Working memory capacity estimates change with age.
source: Furthermore, developmental studies have found that that working memory capacity estimates change with age (Simmering and Perone, 2012; Simmering, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from developmental studies.

claim: A subject's coding efficiency may improve during childhood.
source: A speculative answer is that a subject's coding efficiency – formalized by the reciprocal of parameter α in Equation 7 – may improve during childhood: an increase in coding efficiency reduces the neural cost per unit of precision, which shifts the optimal amount of resource to use for encoding to larger values.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative explanation.

claim: The model comparison indicates that the data provide similar support for both the resource-rational model and the descriptive power-law model, with a small advantage for the resource-rational model.
source: Model comparison based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (Akaike, 1974) indicates that the data provide similar support for both models, with a small advantage for the resource-rational model (ΔAIC = 5.27 ± 0.70; throughout the paper, X ± Y indicates mean ±s.e.m. across subjects).
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: The resource-rational model has a substantial AIC advantage over a fixed-resource model in the equal-precision variant.
source: Consistent with the results obtained with the variable-precision model, we find that the rational model has a substantial AIC advantage over a fixed-resource model (ΔAIC = 43.0 ± 6.8) and is on equal footing with the power-law model (ΔAIC = 2.0 ± 1.7 in favor of the power-law model).
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: All three equal-precision models are outperformed by their variable-precision equivalents by over 100 AIC points.
source: However, all three equal-precision models (fixed resource, power law, rational) are outperformed by their variable-precision equivalents by over 100 AIC points.
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: The fits of the rational model cannot be improved much further without overfitting the data.
source: We find a marginal AIC difference, suggesting that the fits of the rational model cannot be improved much further without overfitting the data (ΔAIC = 3.49 ± 0.93, in favor of the non-parametric model).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a non-parametric model.

claim: Model comparison favors the power-law behavioral cost function over three parameter-free choices.
source: Model comparison favors the original model with AIC differences of 14.0 ± 2.8, 24.4 ± 4.1, and 19.5 ± 3.5, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: The original behavioral cost function outperforms a two-parameter function proposed by Sims (2015).
source: However, this extra flexibility does not increase the goodness of fit sufficiently to justify the additional parameter, as the original model outperforms this variant with an AIC difference of 5.3 ± 1.8.
evidence: This is supported by AIC comparison.

claim: The AIC-based results are consistent with five-fold cross-validation results.
source: Finally, we use five-fold cross validation to verify the AIC-based results reported in this section. We find that they are all consistent (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by cross-validation analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The resource-rational model accounts well for the subject-level error distributions.
source: The model accounts well for the subject-level error distributions (Figure 3A) and the two statistics that summarize these distributions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The model accounts well for the four datasets that were excluded from the main analyses.
source: Although we decided to leave those four datasets out of our main analyses, the model accounts well for them too (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model comparison suggests that subjects distribute their resource near-optimally across items with unequal probing probabilities.
source: Hence, the model comparison suggests quite convincingly that subjects distribute their resource near-optimally across items with unequal probing probabilities, but it is inconclusive regarding the question of whether the total amount of invested resource is fixed or optimized.
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: The resource-rational model cannot reliably be distinguished from Bays' proposal.
source: However, our model cannot reliably be distinguished from the proposal by Bays: either model is preferred in about half of the subjects (our model: 27; Bays: 20) and the subject-averaged AIC difference is negligible (1.8 ± 2.5 in favor of our model).
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: The resource-rational model has a substantial advantage over Emrich et al.'s proposal.
source: Fitting the models to the data from all 47 subjects in E7-E9, we find a substantial advantage of our model over the proposal by Emrich et al., with an AIC difference of 18.0 ± 3.9.
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: The domain of probing probability consists of three potential regimes, each with a different optimal encoding strategy.
source: It can be proven (see Appendix 1) that under these assumptions, the domain of probing probability pi consists of three potential regimes, each with a different optimal encoding strategy (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is proven in Appendix 1 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The only way the model can predict set size effects is through a coupling between N and pi.
source: Therefore, the only way in which the model can predict set size effects is through a coupling between N and pi.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model structure.

claim: In most studies that use a local task, there is a coupling between set size and probing probability.
source: Such a coupling exists in most studies that use a local task. For example, in delayed-estimation tasks, each item is usually equally likely to be probed such that pi = 1/N.
evidence: This is a statement about common experimental designs.

claim: The expected behavioral cost across all items is independent of set size when pi = 1/N and all items are encoded with the same amount of resource.
source: Substituting pi = 1/N in Equation 9, we find that the expected behavioral cost across all items is independent of set size (Figure 2E, left panel, black curve).
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical formulation and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Palmer et al. (1993) reported that 'relevant set size' acts virtually identically to actual set size.
source: Palmer et al. (1993) reported that "relevant set size" (where irrelevance means pi = 0) acts virtually identically to actual set size.
evidence: This is cited from Palmer et al., 1993.

claim: Emrich et al. (2017) found that probing probability was a better predictor of performance than set size.
source: Emrich et al. (2017) independently varied probing probability and set size in their experiment, and found that the former was a better predictor of performance than the latter.
evidence: This is cited from Emrich et al., 2017.

claim: Emrich et al. (2017) hypothesized that set size effects are mediated by probing probability.
source: Based on this, they hypothesized that set size effects are mediated by probing probability.
evidence: This is cited from Emrich et al., 2017.

claim: The predictions of the resource-rational model are qualitatively consistent with the findings of Palmer et al. (1993) and Emrich et al. (2017).
source: The predictions of our model are qualitatively consistent with these findings.
evidence: This is a comparison between model predictions and empirical findings.

claim: The estimation error follows a Von Mises distribution.
source: As the task-relevant feature in delayed-estimation experiments is usually a circular variable (color or orientation), we make the common assumption that ε follows a Von Mises distribution.
evidence: This is a standard modeling assumption for circular variables.

claim: Human subjects tend to perform well on delayed-estimation tasks even when the reward is independent of their performance.
source: As in most psychophysical experiments, human subjects tend to perform well on delayed-estimation tasks even when the reward is independent of their performance.
evidence: This is a general observation about human behavior in psychophysical experiments.

claim: The behavioral cost function is strongly determined by internal incentives.
source: This suggests that the behavioral cost function is strongly determined by internal incentives.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation about human performance.

claim: The expected total cost per item has a unique minimum.
source: The expected total cost per item has a unique minimum (middle panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The optimal amount of resource per item is an increasing function of probing probability.
source: Hence, in this example, the optimal amount of resource per item is an increasing function of its probing probability.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and is a consequence of the cost minimization.

claim: Resource optimization in global tasks is computationally much more demanding than in local tasks.
source: This makes resource optimization computationally much more demanding, because it requires solving an N-dimensional minimization problem instead of N one-dimensional problems.
evidence: This is a consequence of the computational structure of global tasks.

claim: In the change detection simulation at N=2, the cost-minimizing strategy is to encode neither of the items when reward is very low.
source: The results (Figure 5B) show that the cost-minimizing strategy is to encode neither of the items when the amount of reward per correct trial is very low (left panel) and encode them both when reward is high (right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the change detection simulation at N=2, the cost-minimizing strategy is to encode both items when reward is high.
source: The results (Figure 5B) show that the cost-minimizing strategy is to encode neither of the items when the amount of reward per correct trial is very low (left panel) and encode them both when reward is high (right panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the change detection simulation at N=2, there is an intermediate regime in which the optimal strategy is to encode one of the two items, but not the other one.
source: However, interestingly, there is also an intermediate regime in which the optimal strategy is to encode one of the two items, but not the other one (Figure 5B, central panel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the change detection task, it is optimal to encode only a subset of items even when all items are equally likely to change.
source: Hence, just as in the delayed-estimation task, there are conditions in which it is optimal to encode only a subset of items. An important difference, however, is that in the delayed-estimation task this only happens when items have unequal probing probabilities, while in this change detection task it even happens when all items are equally likely to change.
evidence: This is derived from the simulation results.

claim: If two items are encoded in the change detection task, the optimal solution is to encode them with the same amount of resource.
source: However, the results at N = 2 suggest that if two items are encoded, the optimal solution is to encode them with the same amount of resource (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VWM limitations may be driven by a mechanism that minimizes a cost, instead of by a fixed constraint on available encoding resource.
source: The broader implication of our findings is that VWM limitations – and cognitive limitations in general – may be driven by a mechanism that minimizes a cost, instead of by a fixed constraint on available encoding resource.
evidence: This is a broader interpretation of the findings.

claim: Encoding precision in VWM is fundamentally limited by the precision of the sensory input.
source: However, encoding precision in VWM is fundamentally limited by the precision of the sensory input, which is itself limited by irreducible sources of neural noise – such as Johnson noise and Poisson shot noise (Faisal et al., 2008; Smith, 2015) – and suboptimalities in early sensory processing (Beck et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroscience literature.

claim: The total amount of resource must have an upper limit because the brain is a finite entity.
source: However, as the brain is a finite entity, the total amount of resource must obviously have an upper limit.
evidence: This is a logical statement about physical constraints.

claim: Task-irrelevant stimuli are sometimes automatically encoded.
source: However, there is evidence that task-irrelevant stimuli are sometimes automatically encoded (Yi et al., 2004; Shin and Ma, 2016), perhaps because in natural environments few stimuli are ever completely irrelevant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Part of the variability in resource assignment may be systematic, such as particular colors and orientations being encoded with higher precision than others.
source: Part of this variability is possibly a result of stochastic factors, but part of it may also be systematic – for example, particular colors and orientations may be encoded with higher precision than others (Bae et al., 2014; Girshick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Maintaining exactly equal resource assignment across cortical regions may itself be a costly process.
source: One way to reconcile this apparent suboptimality with the otherwise normative theory is to postulate that maintaining exactly equal resource assignment across cortical regions may itself be a costly process; under such a cost, it could be optimal to allow for some variability in resource assignment.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative explanation.

claim: Zhang and Luck (2011) and Nassar et al. (2018) did not find evidence for a difference in encoding precision between low- and high-precision conditions.
source: Neither of the two studies found evidence for a difference in encoding precision between the low- and high-precision conditions.
evidence: This is cited from Zhang and Luck (2011) and Nassar et al. (2018).

claim: The experimental manipulations in the studies by Zhang and Luck and Nassar et al. may not have been strong enough to measure an effect of incentive.
source: In particular, the simulation results suggest that the experimental manipulations in the studies by Zhang and Luck and Nassar et al. may not have been strong enough to measure an effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of simulation results.

claim: Fougnie et al. (2016) criticized the study by Zhang and Luck and found an effect when using an experimental design with stronger incentives.
source: Indeed, another study has criticized the study by Zhang and Luck on exactly this point and did find an effect when using an experimental design with stronger incentives (Fougnie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from Fougnie et al. (2016).

claim: Data from experiments E1-E7 and Matlab code for model fitting and simulations are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/dryad.nf5dr6c.
source: Data from experiments E1-E7 (Table 1) and Matlab code for model fitting and simulations are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.5061/dryad.nf5dr6c.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.
